Figure 6b shows the cycling performance of the pouch cell at different temperatures. At 25 \u00b0C, the pouch cell provides a capacity of 1.18 Ah. As the temperature decreases, we verify the possibility of its operation at low temperatures, at -50 \u00b0C, the pouch cell still provides a capacity of 0.79 Ah (107 Wh kg $^{-1}$ ), demonstrating a significantly better low-temperature adaptability than that of conventional electrolytes. Moreover, even at -50 \u00b0C, the charge/discharge curve maintains a stable voltage plateau (Fig. 6c). Figure 6d shows the cycling performance of the pouch cell at -20 \u00b0C with 94.1% capacity retention after 300 cycles. In addition, in order to visually verify the practical application potential, the LED lights are continuously powered at a low temperature of -50 \u00b0C. The fully-charged state pouch cells keep the LED lights working for more than 10 hours (Fig. 6e). This demonstration confirms that the CIE has good prospects for practical applications, especially at low temperatures. We further compare our results with some previously reported low-temperature sodium-ion pouch cells (Fig. 6f, Table S6) $^{26,52-58}$ , and our work is comparable to most of the advanced reported works, which fully proves that the CIE developed by us has important application value for SIBs in cold environments. According to the frontier molecular orbital theory, the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) energy level of the selected additive molecules should be higher than that of the solvent molecules to enable the reduction of additive molecules on the cathode material surface to form the SEI film. Nitrile is one of the promising electrolyte additives for the following reasons: First, the reduction potential of nitrile is lower than that of carbonate solvents, which can induce the formation of SEI film with a low impedance on the surface of the cathode material. Design and performance of the functional electrolyte\\nThe combination of EC and EMC has been widely adopted for the formulation of carbonate-based electrolytes in commercial pouch lithium-ion batteries, enabling stable charge-discharge performance over more than 1000 cycles at ambient temperature. However, this simple solvent mixture has been shown to be insufficient for achieving long-term cycling stability in pouch SIBs [20]. In sodium-ion batteries, conventional electrolytes fail to address sluggish ion kinetics at low temperatures and interfacial instability at elevated temperatures, highlighting the urgent need for the development of functional electrolyte additives (Fig. 2a). Therefore, the design of a wide-temperature electrolyte system is guided by the following structural considerations. The rigid benzene ring, as a conjugated system, possesses inherently stable chemical properties. The unique electronic structure of benzenesulfonyl compounds is expected to enhance the thermal stability of pouch batteries, thereby reducing the risk of thermal runaway. Moreover, this structural motif has also been employed to address sluggish ion transport kinetics under low-temperature conditions [21]. Meanwhile, anhydride additives have demonstrated multiple interfacial benefits: they can suppress gas evolution during cycling [22], increase the inorganic content of the SEI layer [15], and eliminate trace moisture in the electrolyte, which in turn mitigates the hydrolysis of phosphate species [16,23] (Fig. 2b). Therefore, it holds the potential to reduce the internal resistance of the battery, enhance rate capability, facilitate more efficient sodium-ion transport under low-temperature conditions, and promote improved electrochemical stability at elevated temperatures. Design and performance of the functional electrolyte\nThe combination of EC and EMC has been widely adopted for the formulation of carbonate-based electrolytes in commercial pouch lithium-ion batteries, enabling stable charge-discharge performance over more than 1000 cycles at ambient temperature. However, this simple solvent mixture has been shown to be insufficient for achieving long-term cycling stability in pouch SIBs [20]. In sodium-ion batteries, conventional electrolytes fail to address sluggish ion kinetics at low temperatures and interfacial instability at elevated temperatures, highlighting the urgent need for the development of functional electrolyte additives (Fig. 2a). Therefore, the design of a wide-temperature electrolyte system is guided by the following structural considerations. The rigid benzene ring, as a conjugated system, possesses inherently stable chemical properties. The unique electronic structure of benzenesulfonyl compounds is expected to enhance the thermal stability of pouch batteries, thereby reducing the risk of thermal runaway. Moreover, this structural motif has also been employed to address sluggish ion transport kinetics under low-temperature conditions [21]. Meanwhile, anhydride additives have demonstrated multiple interfacial benefits: they can suppress gas evolution during cycling [22], increase the inorganic content of the SEI layer [15], and eliminate trace moisture in the electrolyte, which in turn mitigates the hydrolysis of phosphate species [16,23] (Fig. 2b). Therefore, it holds the potential to reduce the internal resistance of the battery, enhance rate capability, facilitate more efficient sodium-ion transport under low-temperature conditions, and promote improved electrochemical stability at elevated temperatures.
